articles.text: On Friday, December 5, the Piedmont Police Department hosted a holiday gift drive in front of the police station in an effort to fill the Community Service Officer’s (CSO) truck bed for those in need. articles.text: With AC Transit’s elimination of bus line 33 cutting off service to much of Piedmont, many families have looked for alternative ways for their children to get to school. In response, the community group Piedmont Unplugged is launching a “bike bus” on Friday, January 9, offering students a supervised group ride from Bear Park to Havens Elementary. The “bike bus” will be meeting at 8 am and leaving at 8:10 am. The bike bus will be led by experienced parents and accompanied by a Piedmont Police Department officer on its first day, helping students learn street safety and the rules of the road as they ride together. Helmets and bikes are required, and students can park their bikes on the Havens campus without needing a lock. AC Transit’s recent service redesign replaced line 33 with line 88, which now stops at Highland Avenue but no longer reaches deeper into Piedmont. For many families, the reduced access has made it difficult for students to take the bus to school. Line 18 now serves the corridor between downtown Oakland and Montclair. For resident Danielle Horowitz, founder of Piedmont Unplugged, the loss of line 33 was a turning point. Her family had been preparing for their children to ride the bus to school this year. articles.text: Each year, the school calendar shapes the rhythm of learning, family life, and teacher workload across our district. With that in mind, many parents — myself included — were hopeful that the newly proposed calendars for the next two school years might reflect adjustments the community has expressed interest in: a slightly later August start, a midweek first day, and a less fragmented spring schedule. Instead, the new calendars reflect minimal positive change from previous versions. Under our current system, the calendar is negotiated entirely within the teachers’ union contract, with the School Board’s role limited to approving the final product rather than helping shape it. There has also been recent community discussion on this topic, including thoughtful perspectives shared by both parents and APT. My intention is not to revisit disagreements, but to focus on how we might approach this process more collaboratively in the future. I understand that APT enters calendar negotiations with real needs: predictability, equitable teaching assignments, and stability. At the same time, families and students have needs as well - smoother pacing, more cohesive semesters, and a gentler transition from summer into the school year. Our current approach makes it difficult to balance these needs in a holistic way. Many nearby high-performing districts — including Palo Alto, Orinda, and Acalanes — have found ways to balance these interests more effectively. Their Boards maintain oversight of the academic calendar while still centering teacher voice. As a result, they have adopted more sensible semester splits, with 84-86 instructional days in the fall and 94-96 in the spring, while still scheduling finals before winter break. This demonstrates that teacher priorities and community priorities can coexist within a collaborative process. articles.text: Piedmont is in the final phase of the repaving portion of its 2025 street rehabilitation project. Work began last week on five roads, which are expected to be finished by the end of this week. The final phase includes repaving 10 streets and restriping an additional 32 to improve road quality across the city. The $1.5 million project is funded primarily by Alameda County transportation sales tax revenue and state transportation funds. Repaving has been split into two phases, one in October and the other in early November. The first phase focused on streets in better condition, which received chip and slurry sealing treatments to repair cracks and other surface-level issues. Phase two includes streets needing more extensive work. These roads are receiving a combination of grind-and-pave treatment, in which the top layer of asphalt is removed and replaced, as well as full reconstruction on sections where both the pavement and underlying base material must be rebuilt. The remaining steps in the project include completing paving on streets that were dug out last week and adding striping to the newly paved roads. articles.text: Ansel is a 4-year-old Lynx point with striking blue eyes and an expressive face that has earned him the nickname of “the least mysterious cat ever” from his foster. Although shy at first, he warms quickly, gaining confidence from gentle affection. Once settled, he becomes a sweet, chatty, companion who offers soft trills, chirpy meows, and the sweetest paw pokes to let you know he would like some attention. He enjoys soft petting, cuddles, and being held, often melting into your arms. At night, he loves sleeping beside his person, and during the day he alternates between cozy naps and playful bursts of activity. articles.text: While the University of California and California State University systems do not include SAT or ACT scores as part of their application, there are schools across the country that are reinstating the once-ubiquitous standardized tests as a college admissions requirement. From Caltech to MIT, and at many other campuses nationwide, standardized testing is back. For students intending to apply to schools that are test-blind, like the UCs and CSUs, or test-required, the decision to prepare for and take standardized tests is easy. But for students who have colleges that are test-optional on their lists, deciding whether or not to take the SAT and/or ACT is more nuanced. When a college is test-optional for admissions, it means that the test is one part of the application that admissions officers evaluate. Like the student’s essay, extracurricular activities, course rigor, leadership, and AP test scores, SAT or ACT test scores can strengthen the overall application. Even at schools that are officially test-optional, there are some colleges whose admission data (as reported in the Common Data Set) indicates that students who submit scores are admitted at a much higher rate than those who do not. Standardized test scores also may be required for university-based merit scholarship consideration. If your student’s college application strategy includes chasing merit money, a solid test score can quite literally pay off. Some schools, like University of Chicago and Drexel University, have a no-harm test policy. The admissions officers at schools with this policy indicate that SAT or ACT scores will be considered only if they are an asset to a student’s application. Admissions officers at test-required schools like Brown University and University of Texas at Austin have been outspoken regarding how standardized tests help demonstrate readiness for college level work. Furthermore, for students interested in pursuing STEM disciplines, these tests quantify preparatory math skills on which admissions decisions may be based. Understanding the state of standardized testing can help families shape a test preparation plan that allows the student to submit the strongest application possible. Karen Shopoff Rooff is Director of College Consulting at Study Smarter. articles.text: Girl Scout Troop 32125 shops for their adopted family, a single mom with a toddler and a baby, at Target. Girl Scout Troop 32125, a group of 2nd graders from Wildwood Elementary, went shopping on Wednesday, December 3 for an adopted family. The Adopt-aFamily program is organized by Brighter Beginnings, an East Bay non-profit providing families in resource-poor communities with the support and help needed to raise children with healthy and happy futures. Troop 32125 visited the Target store in Emeryville and broke into teams of two or three Girl Scouts and an adult. Each team shopped for a member of the family: a single mom, her two year-old daughter, and a newborn baby. First names and ages are included in the family bios, but the interaction is otherwise anonymous. Seven-year-old Girl Scout Siena Paley described her experience: “I felt like I was doing the right thing. I felt good. I thought the family needed more than what we were able to give them and I feel bad that they don’t have everything they need. But it’s a good start! And I can’t wait to hear what the baby’s name is!” “On the surface, this is a nice, hands-on way for our troop to give back to less fortunate members of our community,” said Troop Leader Maggie Pickavance. “Each team had a budget to shop with and had to calculate the prices of their gifts. They had to make some choices between buying a coat or buying a toy and had to weigh the difference between a want and a need.” After shopping, the troop wrapped all the gifts, which was an exciting project in and of itself. Items were then dropped off at Brighter Beginnings, where they’re distributed to families. Girl Scout cookie season will begin online on January 12 and booths will start appearing on February 4. Proceeds from cookie sales provide the funds for Girl Scout troops to operate, but also to support community service efforts throughout the year.

Community members are invited to drop off new, unwrapped toys in the barrels in front of the school Monday-Friday from 8 a.m. to 12 p.m. through December 12. PPS is located at 401 Hampton Road on Hampton Field beside the tennis courts. “Tangible giving opportunities like this help our children learn, in a hands-on way, what it means to care for others. Those are the values that have always guided PPS,” said PPS board member Sandy Fedor. “All donations will go directly to Toys for Tots, which distributes gifts to families who might otherwise go without.” The City of Piedmont is ending PPS’s residency in the building that Piedmont residents built for the school, making this year’s tradition of giving back especially meaningful. “Even though the future of Piedmont Play School is uncertain, we feel strongly about contributing to the community,” added Fedor. Piedmont Play School welcomes donations from all members of the community. Together, families, neighbors and friends can help make the season brighter for children across the East Bay. Girl Scout Troop adopts family for holidays Girl Scout Troop 32125 shops for their adopted family, a single mom with a toddler and a baby, at Target. Girl Scout Troop 32125, a group of 2nd graders from Wildwood Elementary, went shopping on Wednesday, December 3 for an adopted family. The Adopt-aFamily program is organized by Brighter Beginnings, an East Bay non-profit providing families in resource-poor communities with the support and help needed to raise children with healthy and happy futures. Troop 32125 visited the Target store in Emeryville and broke into teams of two or three Girl Scouts and an adult. Each team shopped for a member of the family: a single mom, her two year-old daughter, and a newborn baby. First names and ages are included in the family bios, but the interaction is otherwise anonymous. Seven-year-old Girl Scout Siena Paley described her experience: “I felt like I was doing the right thing. I felt good. I thought the family needed more than what we were able to give them and I feel bad that they don’t have everything they need. But it’s a good start! And I can’t wait to hear what the baby’s name is!” “On the surface, this is a nice, hands-on way for our troop to give back to less fortunate members of our community,” said Troop Leader Maggie Pickavance. “Each team had a budget to shop with and had to calculate the prices of their gifts. They had to make some choices between buying a coat or buying a toy and had to weigh the difference between a want and a need.” After shopping, the troop wrapped all the gifts, which was an exciting project in and of itself. Items were then dropped off at Brighter Beginnings, where they’re distributed to families. Girl Scout cookie season will begin online on January 12 and booths will start appearing on February 4. Proceeds from cookie sales provide the funds for Girl Scout troops to operate, but also to support community service efforts throughout the year. articles.text: Within the Piedmont High School community, English teacher Beth Black is known for her ability to lift students up. She can turn a hesitant ninth grader into a confident writer, she brings a steady, calm authority to seniors preparing for their next steps, and as the inaugural head coach of the Girls Flag Football team, she has become a defining presence in one of the fastest growing sports in the country. Coach Black has spent more than 24 years teaching English and journalism at Piedmont High School. She guides students through literature, analysis, revision, and the work of finding their own voice. Many return years later to share that something they learned from her stayed with them, moments that reflect the care and intention she brings to her teaching. Sports have always played an important role in her life. She grew up in Ohio in a family where football was part of everyday conversation. At the University of Toledo, she became a competitive dancer, honing the discipline and focus that now guide her coaching style. She also played recreational flag football in college and discovered just how strategic and engaging the sport can be. When girls f lag football became an official high school sport in California in 2023, Coach Black stepped forward to establish the program at Piedmont. She partnered with teacher and assistant coach Haley Adams to build the program from the ground up, creating a welcoming space for experienced athletes and newcomers alike. Their work resonated immediately. Interest surged, tryouts filled quickly, and the program became one of the most popular and inclusive teams on campus. Piedmont now fields three full levels. The varsity team brings experience and competitive skill. The JV team supports developing athletes. The frosh team gives newcomers a place to learn the game and grow with confidence. This structure has produced allleague players and created opportunities that did not exist even a few years ago. For Coach Black, the most rewarding moments are the ones when a player suddenly sees the game differently. A route comes together, a read makes sense, or a young athlete trusts her ability for the first time. These breakthroughs reflect the confidence and growth she works to build. Whether she is guiding a student through a college essay, helping a reporter refine a story for The Piedmont Highlander, or supporting her players during practice, Coach Black brings steady commitment and genuine care. Her influence reaches from the classroom to the newsroom to the field, and many students discover new confidence because she helps them see what they can achieve. Coach Black reflected further on her coaching journey and the rise of girls’ flag football. girls like me who grew up playing football with boys but had no real opportunity to join a team, this is a long-awaited change. For many years, girls had to become the sideline supporters instead of the players. Now the door is open, and the message is clear: of course you can do this. Q: What core values do you instill in your players? A: One value is to try something new, even in high school. Many of our players come from soccer, volleyball, water polo, and other sports, and they are discovering they can be good at something completely new. Another key value is teamwork. Football requires teamwork in a way that few other sports do. And finally, football teaches you to own your space. You have a right to that space on the field, and if you get there first, it is yours. That awareness and confidence are important lessons. Q: What has been the most rewarding or exciting moment so far, on or off the field? A: Watching the growth of players over three years has been incredibly rewarding. articles.text: Photo by Gary Sexton Installation view of Contemporary Painting in Papua New Guinea: Mathias Kauage and His Family A rare and unique exhibition featuring artwork by contemporary Papuan artist Mathias Kauage is on display at the de Young, one of the fine arts museums of San Francisco, now through March 2026. Kauage is regarded as the leading figure of contemporary art in Papua New Guinea and exhibited internationally in Europe, America and Australia regularly before he died in 2003. The exhibition features four paintings from the de Young’s permanent collection by Mathias Kauage and his family, on view for the first time. Born in 1944 in a remote village in Papua New Guinea’s remote highlands, the artist moved to Port Moreseby, the country’s capital, as a teenager. He began drawing at a young age when he was inspired by the work of Timothy Akis, the first Papuan artist to hold a western-style exhibition. Under the mentorship of German artist Gerogina Beier at the National Arts School in Port Moresby, Kauage began to develop his own distinctive style and find his preferred medium of acrylic on canvas. He also learned and mastered printmaking techniques, woodcuts and copper-beating. Kauage is most famous for his acrylic on canvas paintings and murals, which are highlighted in this exhibit. His works famously focused on how technology has impacted life in remote Papua New Guinea, and his later works addressed societal issues such as the onset of the HIV/AIDS epidemic. In the late 1970s, Kauage and his wife Elisabet led the contemporary arts movement in the newly independent Papua New Guinea. His works are currently held in the National Gallery of Australia, the National Gallery of Papua New Guinea, the British Museum and the Gallery of Modern Art, Glasgow, but are less often on display in western museums, making the de Young’s exhibition a rarity. To learn more, visit https:// www.famsf.org/exhibitions/papua-new-guinea-mathias-kauage.

articles.text: Rhythmix Cultural Center will open a new group exhibition next month showcasing artwork created by frontline staff of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. Art Comes From Art, Comes From Art runs January 17 through February 22 and features seven artists who work at the Legion of Honor and the de Young while maintaining active creative practices of their own. The exhibition is organized by Natalie Jeng, PHS class of 2019, and highlights new pieces inspired directly by the museums’ collections, architecture and visitors. Works range from beadwork and painting to digital illustration, cartooning and brush-and-ink comics, reflecting the varied perspectives found within the museum community. The exhibition’s title nods to Art Comes from Art, the 2025 Wayne Thiebaud exhibition at the Legion of Honor, Jeng said. “[The exhibition title] echoes Thiebaud’s belief that all art exists in dialogue with what has come before,” she said. “In a moment when cultural institutions everywhere are navigating challenges, this show focuses on something uplifting: how much inspiration museum staff draw from the art they help steward, and how that influence flows back into the Bay Area’s artistic community.” The Rhythmix exhibition aims to celebrate that “circular exchange of inspiration” by presenting artwork shaped by daily encounters with masterpieces and with colleagues who share a passion for art, she added. Independently organized, the show offers the public a rare look at the creative lives of museum staff members whose behindthe-scenes roles support the Bay Area’s cultural institutions. By shifting their own work into a gallery space, participating artists highlight the ways museums continually influence and energize local artistic communities. Participating artists include Daniele Erville, Nancy Jean Guerrero, Natalie Jeng, Sam Piro, David Manzanares Taffolla, Marvin Velasco and David Wong. An opening reception will be held January 17 from 5 to 8 p.m. at Rhythmix Cultural Center, 2513 Blanding Avenue Gallery hours are scheduled for February 8, 15 and 22 from noon to 3 p.m. More information is available at rhythmix.org/upcoming-exhibits. articles.text: Grammy award-winning violinist Mads Tolling returns to SFJAZZ this Saturday and Sunday, December 14 and 15, to perform four concerts featuring ‘jazzified’ traditional carols from Nordic countries. Tolling is a Danish-American violinist and composer and twotime Grammy award-winner, best known for his work with the Turtle Island Quartet, Stanley Clarke, Bob Weir, and local groups including the all-star San Francisco String Trio. After about nine years with Turtle Island Quartet and several years touring with bassist Stanley Clarke’s band, Tolling branched out to lead his own groups. He is a regular performer at the SFJAZZ Center, having first performed at the center in 2010 in a double bill with Regina Carter. He collaborated with the Grateful Dead’s Bob Weir and the Wolf Bros. on projects more recently. This weekend, Tolling celebrates the season with reimagined Mads Tolling versions of carols from Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Finland and Iceland, blending the mysticism, customs and sounds of the Nordic countries along with the joy and soul of American jazz. articles.text: Revered maestro Riccardo Muti Revered maestro Riccardo Muti and his beloved Chicago Symphony Orchestra will reconvene in Berkeley for a program of popular orchestra gems on Saturday, January 17. Muti, who turns 84 this year, stepped down as the Orchestra’s music director to assume the role of Music Director Emeritus for Life in 2023, but rejoins the musicians for this special evening performance on UC Berkeley’s campus. The New York Times hails Muti’s legacy, calling the orchestra “all power and finesse” under his tenure, saying “he barely had to move for the players to unleash torrents of stupendous, beautifully balanced sound.” Muti excels at Brahms and will conduct the composer’s majestic Fourth Symphony; Stravinsky’s delightful suite from the ballet The Fairy’s Kiss; and Ravel’s magnificent Boléro, which builds the concert to a volcanic climax. A full program book will be available approximately one week before the performance. The concert, organized by Cal Performances, begins at 8 p.m. Visit https://calperformances.org/ to purchase tickets.

pages.text: 18 18 Wednesday, December 10, 2025 The Musical Gourmet Famous Freddy By Joseph Gold You probably don’t recognize his name, but Freddie Potter really was the most popular violinist of all time. The piano world had Paderewski and the violin world had Freddie Potter. That wasn’t his real name, however. It is a translation. Freddie was born in Vienna on February 2, 1875. Quite coincidentally another contender for greatest violinist of all time was born on the same date. His name was Joseph Heifetz who later changed his last name to Heifitz. And now to Freddie. In addition to being the most popular violinist of all time, Freddie was a fantastic composer. He was also a prevaricator – a very charming liar. He simply made up stories and related them with conviction. As is the case with many musicians, he was a child genius. After winning first prize at the Vienna Conservatory, he won first prize at the Paris Conservatory. Soon after, he was engaged to concertize in America, but the concert tour was not an overwhelming success. Despite the early promise of this gifted musician, his career did not materialize. He decided to audition for a violin position with the Vienna Philharmonic but it was a failure in every aspect. He liked to tell people that he The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet studied art in an art academy. He was very good at drawing stick figures. Then he enrolled in medical school but probably didn’t graduate because he never became a doctor. At some time he actually became an officer in the Austrian army and got married. His career blossom and he composed countless popular violin pieces. His wife took 100% of the credit for his success. Freddie decided to move to the United States. W hen Aust r ia became involved in World War I, Freddie decided he’d better return to his army unit. He was an officer, after all. He claimed that he was wounded in the battle of Tannenburg, and even wrote a book about his adventures describing his leg injury. It was impossible to ascertain if he actually was injured. Freddie was great at saying whatever was good at the time. Both of his parents were Jewish. His wife, however, was a bigot. She denied Freddie’s Jewish background and often said: “My husband does not have one drop of Jewish blood”. A famous response to this statement was: “He must be anemic.” Mrs. Potter often stated that she insisted that Freddie practice. She was, after all, responsible for his concert success. It was known that Freddie did not practice while on tour. The truth is, he didn’t need to practice. His concert schedule was 13 concerts in a row with one day off. Along the way, he composed countless popular pieces but denied that he was the composer. A suspicious music critic demanded to see the original manuscripts, and Freddie was forced to admit that he composed all of them. An international scandal ensued. But the public loved Freddie so much they embraced him even more. His career continued at the highest level until he was severely injured in a traffic accident. That was just about the end of his career. He was lucky to be alive. When he died in 1962 all the newspaper headlines read: “greatest violinist of all time dies.” Have you figured out who Freddie Potter was? His original first name was Friedrich. That’s Frederick in English. The diminutive is Freddie and in German, it’s Fritz. Potter is an English version of Kreisler. That’s it… Fritz Kreisler… the most popular violinist of all time. Caricature of a famous violinist by another famous musician, Enrico Caruso. Democracy is not a spectator sport! articles.text: Noomi Rapace in The Girl Who Kicked the Hornet’s Nest More than a decade after the Millennium trilogy first electrified readers and audiences, The Girl Who Kicked the Hornet’s Nest remains a reminder of just how indelible Noomi Rapace’s Lisbeth Salander truly is. For many who discovered Stieg Larsson’s novels in the summer of 2010, curiosity about the films centered on a single question: who could possibly play Salander? The answer, as it turned out, was an actress who would go on to build an extraordinary global career. Long before her recent psychological-sci-fi turn in Constellation, Rapace’s breakout performance in The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo set a standard that has rarely been matched. Her Lisbeth is fierce and fragile, wounded and impenetrable, a character who communicates more with a single glance than with a page of dialogue. Rapace gives her a coiled, electric stillness, masking a history of trauma with razor intelligence and a silent, unyielding will. All three films unfold in Sweden, and though the first can be watched on its own as a taut murder mystery, the second and third chapters lock together. To fully appreciate Hornet’s Nest, it is essential to start at the beginning. The trilogy’s world is dense with intrigue and shadowy institutions, threaded through with violence, corruption, and a constant sense of danger. At the center, always, is Salander: hacker, survivor, and a counterforce to the institutional rot that has defined her life. Her gift for navigating the digital underworld, her alliances with fellow hackers with names like Plague, and her relentless pursuit of the truth give the films a propulsive urgency. The battle she wages against a system determined to erase her is as harrowing as anything in contemporary thrillers. When the trilogy ends—on the page or on screen—what lingers is a wish for more: one more book, one more film, one more glimpse into the mind of a character who reshaped the modern thriller. There were rumors, once, of a fourth manuscript left on Larsson’s laptop, but his sudden passing, before the first novel was even published, left that hope unresolved. Hollywood eventually tried its hand at the series, with David Fincher directing an English-language remake of The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo. But Rapace’s interpretation remains singular. Watching Hornet’s Nest today, especially in light of her recent work, you see how this role launched one of the most intriguing actresses of her generation— one still drawn to stories of identity, resilience, and the dark edges of human experience. The Girl Who Kicked the Hornet’s Nest endures because Lisbeth Salander endures. And with Rapace, it never feels over. The Girl Who Kicked the Hornet’s Nest. Directed by Daniel Alfredson. Starring Noomi Rapace, Michael Nyqvist, Annika Hallin, Erika Berger and Micke Spreitz. Released in 2010. 2 hrs., 35 min. Rated R. Streaming on Prime

articles.text: Tangled is a bright, buoyant retelling of the Brothers Grimm story of Rapunzel, shaped into a Disney fantasy-musical perfect for tween audiences. Mandy Moore voices the “lost princess,” stolen as an infant from the King and Queen of Corona by the vain and manipulative Gothel (Donna Murphy). Posing as Rapunzel’s mother, Gothel has kept her hidden in a tower for 18 years, guarded only by a chameleon companion whose shifting colors mirror the girl’s moods. Gothel’s motive is simple: Rapunzel’s impossibly long, golden hair possesses a magical healing power that keeps the old crone forever young. As long as the girl stays isolated, Gothel remains ageless. Everything changes when Flynn Ryder (Zachary Levi), a charming rogue on the run after stealing a tiara, climbs through Rapunzel’s window while looking for a hiding place. She promptly knocks him out with a frying pan, but soon strikes a bargain with him. For years, Rapunzel has watched lanterns rise in the distance on her birthday, unaware they are sent skyward by her grieving parents. She convinces Flynn to guide her to the kingdom of Corona so she can finally see the world beyond her tower walls. The adventure that follows is filled with Disney verve: chase scenes, a flooding cave, run-ins with palace guards, the formidable Gothel, and a scene-stealing horse named Maximus. Through it all, Rapunzel discovers her courage, her identity, and her long-buried connection to the royal family. The ending delivers precisely what a fairy tale promises: Rapunzel’s return, a joyful reunion with her parents, and a royal wedding that brings the story full circle. With its humor, heart, and memorable music, Tangled remains one of Disney’s modern animated standouts. Tangled. Directed by Nathan Greno and Byron Howard. Voices of Mandy Moore, Zachary Levi and Donna Murphy. Released in 2010. 1 hr., 41 min. Rated PG. Streaming on Prime, Disney+, Fandango and Apple. What follows is one of the most tender, visually striking, and thematically rich animated films of the last quarter-century. During a violent storm, a blazing object crashes into the ocean off the Maine coast. Soon after, nine-year-old Hogarth Hughes (Eli Marienthal), a bright, lonely kid whose single mother Annie (Jennifer Aniston) works nights at a diner, wanders into the woods and discovers the source: a towering, metal-eating robot, voiced by Vin Diesel. Nearly electrocuted while feeding on a power station, the self-sacrifice that cements the film’s enduring message: “You are who you choose to be.” Yet the closing moments offer a hint that this may not be the end after all. Beautifully animated—handdrawn characters paired with CGI for the robot—The Iron Giant evokes the warmth and artistic ambition of Studio Ghibli while delivering an unmistakably American story about fear, friendship, and moral choice. articles.text: There was a large turnout of 26 readers on the patio at the Piedmont Community Hall on a cool November 3 for the monthly First Mondays Reading Group discussion. The group was there to talk about their December book, Differ We Must: How Lincoln Succeeded in a Divided America written by NPR’s Morning Edition host Steve Inskeep. The 2023 book examines Abraham Lincoln’s leadership through his interactions with 16 different people, many with whom he had disagreements. Some are wellknown people, but others are obscure. They range from William Seward to Cheyenne Chief Lean Bear. Inskeep uses these people to describe how Lincoln navigated a deeply divided nation. The book’s title comes from a letter that Lincoln wrote to his friend Joshua Speed. In it, Lincoln rebuked Speed for not opposing slavery. He wrote, “If, for this, we must differ, differ we must.” The book tells how Lincoln’s willingness to engage with those with whom he disagreed was crucial to his success. Additionally, Lincoln was a politician. Inskeep shows that because Lincoln was willing to engage in politics, meeting and working with critics, that he was able to keep the union united and lead the social revolution that ended slavery in our country. The acoustics inside the Community Hall can sometimes create hearing issues for the large group and they decided to try an experiment. Ivy Sandoval from the Recreation Department provided a wireless microphone and the readers passed it around during the discussion for them to share their views. The group thought that with the countless books that have been written about Lincoln it was hard to image this book would provide something new. However, for some, it was a totally different Lincoln story and very satisfying. This history was not only based on Lincoln’s actions, but also on others’ lives and voices too. The politics were fascinating and there was so much going on that Lincoln had to contend with. The readers liked that Lincoln was a “people person” as well as a “political creature.” He tempered his idealism and tailored his communications and actions for his audiences to accomplish what he needed to get done. He listened to everyone and then made his discissions. Additionally, the other people that Inskeep profiles had their own stories and they provided the readers with a better understanding of the times. Readers enjoyed some of these people as much as Lincoln. While most readers enjoyed the book, some had to differ. They felt there was too much detail and the “minutia” was more than they wanted. They were disappointed with the book and felt its introduction promised more than Inskeep delivered regarding solutions to our country’s current issues. Some readers didn’t see the relevance of minor characters. They wondered why Lincoln’s Illinois barber, the Native American chief, and some others were included, but the readers found it interesting that the barber was originally from Haiti. The narrative may have been interesting, but it could also be confusing at times. It seemed inevitable that the discussion would move to our nation’s current situation and political divide. Today seems to be another time when history is repeating itself. How can we hold conflicting, contradictory views and somehow reconcile them within ourselves? How could Jefferson proclaim that all men are created equal and be a slave owner? How can we be a “nation of immigrants” and treat immigrants so harshly? Is there a solution other than civil war to keep the country together? That was Lincoln’s primary goal, but it was voiced that Trump is no Lincoln. Politicians are putting self-interest over the country’s needs. Every generation has its own challenges, but ignorance and bigotry haven’t gone away. Inskeep implied that we need to have conversations and work together to resolve our differences, but neither he nor the readers seemed to have answers for making it really happen. The group did have a solution regarding the use of the wireless microphone for improving their conversation. Next month they will start the discussion by passing the microphone around the readers’ circle for each person to express their thoughts about the book and then let the conversation have a free flowing back and forth to understand their different perspectives more fully. Maybe that’s what our country needs, too. The readers had previously selected Cry, the Beloved County by Alan Paton for their January book and The Wide Wide Sea: Imperial Ambition, First Contact and the Fateful Final Voyage of Captain James Cook by Hampton Sides for their February read. After Darby Gregg’s presentation of three fiction candidates the group selected Harlem Shuffle by Colson Whitehead for their March book. It was a chilly day, so the readers took a group photo inside the Community Hall. The group will meet at the Community Hall for their next discussion on January 5th at 1:30 p.m. New readers are welcome and there is no fee to participate, Register at https://bit.ly/3R86PP4. Among those participating in the First Monday Reading Group’s discussion were Heidi Schmidt, Sarah Johnson, Bella Almanzan, Ken Young, Adrienne Hamlin, Martin Levy, Lisa Euphrat, Darby Gregg, Rich Siegel, Orrel Lanter, Mary Carter, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Alicia Rivera, Dick Carter, and discussion leader Priscilla Wanerus. The group was pleased that Rob White, Marj Blackwell, and Evie Stilwell were with them for the first time.

articles.text: How could the upcoming movie possibly be a success? It was to be filmed by Columbia, a second-class studio. MGM loaned Clark Gable out to star in the production, though he didn’t want to do it. His co-star, Claudette Colbert, didn’t want to do it either, and when filming was completed, she called it “the worst picture ever made.” Columbia had low expectations when they released it—but guess what? It went on to win all five major Academy Awards: Best Picture, Best Director, Best Writer, Best Actor, Best Actress. It was 1934’s It Happened One Night, often ranked high among the best American movies ever. Who can resist It Happened One Night? One of the rewarding pleasures of movies is seeing one with friends and then chatting about it when the lights come up. That’s just what the Piedmont Flix Fest, which meets on the second Thursday of each month, offers: a great movie in a comfortable setting, and then a lively discussion of it afterward. The next film in the series is, indeed 1934’s It Happened One Night. Directed by Frank Capra, its plot is similar to that of Roman Holiday, which imitated it 30 years later. In the Capra film, spoiled heiress Ellie Andrews (Claudette Colbert) impetuously marries the gold-digging King Westley, leading her gruff tycoon father (Walter Connolly) to spirit her away on his yacht. After jumping ship, Ellie falls in with cynical newspaper reporter Peter Warne (Clark Gable), who offers to help her reunite with her new husband in exchange for an exclusive story. But during their travels, the reporter finds himself falling for the feisty young heiress. This is a pre-moral-code film, so the sexual innuendos are amusingly frank. It Happened One Night will be screened on Thursday, December 11 at 1:00 p.m. at the Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia Avenue. Doors will open at 12:45 p.m. The movie is free and available to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis. Everyone is welcome to bring snacks or lunch. The next movie in the Piedmont series is the 1992 comedy/ mystery My Cousin Vinny, starring Joe Pesci and Marissa Tomei, who won an Academy Award for her role. It will be shown on January 14th.

He told the walkers that the home had been his wife’s childhood house and that their children built the brick maze as a Covid project using leftover materials from the property. Baringer made it to the summit of Lobuche, rewarded with views of Everest and a “double sun-dog” in the sky, two concentric rainbows ringed around the sun. Back at Lobuche base camp the team said their goodbyes to Jay, who then walked down to Pheriche, beginning the long road home to Colorado. After a needed rest and laundry day, with hot showers in a nearby village, the team prepared to move to their new home: Everest Base Camp. The weather changed abruptly on the climb to Base Camp, and tee-shirts and shorts quickly turned into jackets and gloves. Everest Base Camp’s accommodations were staggering, with large dining tents, cooking tents and hundreds of client tents with 5” thick mattresses. The team spent a day of “puja” or worship at a handcrafted stone altar and brought their mountaineering gear for blessing by the Sherpa high priest in a four-hour joyous ceremony. On Everest, “ice-falls” are some of the most treacherous features. The ice flows rapidly down steep portions of glaciers creating uneven crevassed surfaces amidst 100’ tall ice towers known as seracs. To prepare, guides had the team practice walking across metal ladders with crampons and boots while fully geared up. April 22 marked three weeks into the trip and the first ascent to Camp One, the start of the “rotations” up Everest itself. At 19,500’ the change in elevation caused Baringer to have a sleepless night and a mental battle over concerns he might have developed High-Altitude Pulmonary Edema and sleep apnea. Through that long night, BarBill Baringer crossing a crevasse on a sunny day near Base Camp. inger have serious consideration of canceling his trip. But by the next morning he shook off the night’s doubts with new resolve. On April 24 the team moved up to Camp Two at 21,500’. That day the temperature reached the 90s and required the arduous tasks of removing layers of clothing while climbing. While still suffering from a chest cough and trying to sleep at high elevation, Baringer said he felt his breath through two audible pathways as if he had a hole in his lungs, ear canal or throat. Combined with a gurgle in his lungs and chest pain, he further suspected High-Altitude Pulmonary Edema. The trip’s rotation called for a return to Everest Base camp and Baringer took the opportunity to go to the Himalayan Rescue Association health clinic, where he was diagnosed with pneumonia. Of this development Baringer said, “I was in trouble. Pneumonia and elevation are not a good combination.” The doctor prescribed four medications of steroids and antibiotics in an attempt to purge the pneumonia.The climbing company’s owner Mike Hamill recommended that Baringer rest for four days at Base Camp. By Jay Russell Article originally published in the May 6, 2020 issue of the Piedmont Post. In April 2019 Piedmont climber Bill Baringer was at Lobuche base camp in the Himalayan mountain range, elevation 17,000’. He was recovering from a flu virus and had just twisted an ankle – and he was still 12,000’ away from the Everest summit. On April 14 he attempted to get back on schedule with the rest of the climbing group. Baringer and fellow climber Jay, who was also sick, arose at 2:00 a.m. for a bid at the Lobuche summit with guides Peema and Pemba. Baringer recalled, “It was unreasonably cold, requiring me to wear several layers inside my winter-rated sleeping bag.” Lobuche, a nondescript peak at 20,000’, is similar to Alaska’s Denali in height. It served as the first serious training ground for everyone to test their equipment, technique and feelings. Two hours into the climb Jay’s crampon suddenly detached from his mountaineering boot. This was unprecedented for him, having used the same mountaineering gear in many previous climbs without issue. When the crampon fell off again 10 minutes later, Pemba and Peema made adjustments to secure it. Then, to Baringer and the guides’ dismay, Jay suddenly stopped, and let them know that he wasn’t feeling it and was done. Baringer said, “What do you mean,you’re just quitting this peak right?” Jay replied, “Nope. I’m calling off my trip.” It was Jay’s third attempt at Everest, and he had a two-page resume of climbs around the world. Despite Baringer’s encouragement and support, his new ally and friend waved the white flag to the beast called Everest. Baringer made it to the summit of Lobuche, rewarded with views of Everest and a “double sun-dog” in the sky, two concentric rainbows ringed around the sun. Back at Lobuche base camp the team said their goodbyes to Jay, who then walked down to Pheriche, beginning the long road home to Colorado. After a needed rest and laundry day, with hot showers in a nearby village, the team prepared to move to their new home: Everest Base Camp. The weather changed abruptly on the climb to Base Camp, and tee-shirts and shorts quickly turned into jackets and gloves. articles.text: Montclair Village will shine bright on Thursday, December 11, when the Montclair Village Association welcomes the community to its 23rd annual Holiday Stroll from 4 to 8 p.m. More than 40 Village businesses will offer seasonal treats, shopping and dining promotions, live music, and plenty of holiday cheer. Families can stop by the F&M Bank Family Fun Zone for music and hands-on activities. Santa will be available for Winter Wonderland photos by Leah Marie Studio for $35. Kids can enjoy crafting tables and glowin-the-dark face painting. Entertainment will fill the Village throughout the evening, with performances by The Tap Dancing Christmas Trees, Edna Brewer Jazz Band, The Back Dimples Band, The Zesty Lemons Jazz Combo, and the Jazz Education Ensemble. Shops and restaurants will feature festive sweets, hot beverages, dining specials, unique gifts, and special offers. Vendor Lane returns with more than twenty local artisan vendors. PHS will open the tournament against host school, Acalanes, on Thursday at 7:00 p.m. WORSHIP IN PERSON OR ONLINE SUNDAYS, 10AM DEC 14 11AM Life-Changing Christmas Gifts Celebrating its 22nd year with more than $1M in donations, the Alternative Gift Market at Piedmont Church gives you the opportunity to care for more than just your family and friends at Christmas. These gifts will reach around the world to bring life-giving aid to people who are in desperate need. One hundred percent of your gift will go to the ministries you choose to support. When you purchase a gift in someone’s honor, you can receive a descriptive insert that can be placed into a card to let the person know what you have purchased in their name. Vetted agencies include local organizations like CityTeam, Oakland, giving people experiencing homelessness, poverty, hunger and addiction a chance to find help, hope and a new life. And international organizations like World Neighbors, a group that works to alleviate hunger, poverty and disease in isolated rural villages in Asia, Africa and Latin America. Purchase gifts in person at 11am Sunday, December 14 at Piedmont Church inw Guild Hall with Agency Representatives available to answer questions. Or, scan the QR code to shop from the online catalog.
